ryb.title: Subtractive mixing · paint
ryb.text: Each pigment absorbs part of the light: the more you mix, the darker it gets, and the three primaries make a chromatic black. Complementaries cancel out into grey or brown. Printing uses cyan, magenta and yellow; painters, red, yellow and blue.

rgb.title: Additive mixing · light
rgb.text: Lights are added together: red + green = yellow, and the three primaries make white. Complementaries add up to white. Screens, projectors, stage lighting.

wheel.screenNote: On screen: the relationships between colours, not the exact shade of a tube.

temperature.info: Warming a colour pushes it towards orange; cooling it, towards blue. To grey it without making it muddy, add a little of its complementary.

primaries.title: Primary, secondary, tertiary
primaries.text: In paint, three colours cannot be mixed from others: yellow, red and blue, the primaries. Two primaries mixed make a secondary (orange, violet, green); a primary and its neighbouring secondary, a tertiary.

complements.title: The complementary dilemma
complements.intro: Facing a colour, from the strongest contrast to the softest:

items.complementary: Complementary: the opposite colour. Maximum contrast, sometimes garish.
items.near: Near-complementary: its neighbour. Strong contrast, but softer.
items.shifted: Shifted: further still, pastel or greyed. Light, harmonious contrast.

complements.note: Stripes and checks: the more finely the colours intertwine, the more they vibrate.

temperature.title: Warm and cool, a matter of neighbours
temperature.text: Colours close to orange are warm, those close to blue cool. But temperature is relative: the same colour looks cooler next to a warmer one, and warmer next to a cooler one.
temperature.amongWarmer: Surrounded by a warmer colour, it looks cooler.
temperature.amongCooler: Surrounded by a cooler colour, it looks warmer.
temperature.warmest: It is already the warmest colour.
temperature.coolest: It is already the coolest colour.

values.title: Value and saturation
values.text: A colour has a hue (red, blue…), a value (light or dark) and a saturation (vivid or dull). Two colours of the same value merge in black and white: value is what builds a painting.
values.figure: Value from top to bottom, saturation from left to right

contrasts.title: The 7 colour contrasts
contrasts.intro: Seven ways for colours to talk to each other.

hue.title: Of hue
hue.text: Pure, clear colours side by side: the simplest, most brilliant contrast.

lightDark.title: Light-dark
lightDark.text: Light against dark; it works even without colour.

warmCool.title: Warm-cool
warmCool.text: A warm colour against a cool one: one comes forward, the other recedes.

complementary.title: Complementary
complementary.text: Two opposites on the wheel: they enhance each other side by side and cancel out when mixed.

saturation.title: Of saturation
saturation.text: A vivid colour surrounded by its dulled versions looks even brighter.

extension.title: Of extension
extension.text: Balance comes from areas: a bright colour in small quantity holds its own against a larger dark one.

simultaneous.title: Simultaneous
simultaneous.lead: The eye never sees a colour on its own: it compares it with its surroundings and adds the complementary of the background by itself.
simultaneous.text: The same grey on red seems to turn green; on green, it seems to turn pink. Tick “Connect”: it really is the same grey.
simultaneous.extra: Between complementaries the effect adds up: orange on blue gains in brilliance.
simultaneous.onRed: Grey on vivid red: it leans towards green
simultaneous.onGreen: The same grey on vivid green: it leans towards red
simultaneous.orangeOnBlue: Orange on deep blue: more brilliant

theory.source: To go further: Johannes Itten, The Art of Color (1961), which inspired the 7 contrasts. Texts and illustrations on this page are original.

charts.title: Swatch charts
charts.intro: A swatch chart gathers the tubes of one brand (the “group”). It is exchanged as JSON.
charts.replace: Replace the tubes of these groups
charts.tooBig: File too large (4 MB at most).

rejections.duplicate: duplicate in the file (same group and same name)

fields.name: Trade name of the tube, 60 characters at most. Required.
fields.hex: Colour in sRGB: #RRGGBB (or #RGB). Required. A tube without a valid colour is rejected.
fields.group: Brand, 40 characters at most. At file level it applies to every tube; in a tube, it takes precedence.
fields.pigment: Colour Index code(s): "PB29" or "PR122/PV19", 20 characters at most.
fields.light: Lightfastness, ASTM scale: "I", "II" or "III". Anything else: empty.
fields.opac: Transparency / opacity: "T" transparent, "ST" semi-transparent, "SO" semi-opaque, "O" opaque.
fields.effect: Surface effect: "metal" metallic, "iri" iridescent or pearlescent, "fluo" fluorescent, "none" none (forces an ordinary paint). Empty: the tool infers it from the name or pigment code.

rules.update: A tube with the same group and name as an existing tube updates it (it keeps its ticked state).
rules.owned: New tubes are ticked only if you ask: tick the ones you own, only they are used in the calculations.
rules.invalid: Invalid entries are skipped and listed with their reason before importing.
rules.paste: The JSON can be pasted as is, even surrounded by text or ```json fences.
rules.local: Nothing is sent anywhere: everything stays on this device.

charts.promptHelp: Copy this text into an AI, then attach the manufacturer’s document (PDF, screenshot, table). Paste its answer into “Import” and check the preview.
charts.prompt:
You are preparing a paint swatch chart in JSON for the “Image study” tool. From the manufacturer’s document I attach (table, PDF, text or screenshot), reply ONLY with a valid JSON object: no text before or after, no code fences.

Exact format:
{{format}}

Rules:
1. NEVER invent a value. A tube whose colour is not given in the document is not included. For any other field not given, use an empty string "".
2. "hex": the colour in sRGB on 7 characters (#RRGGBB, upper case). If the document gives RGB, convert it to hexadecimal. If it only gives CMYK, convert with R = 255 × (1 − C) × (1 − K), and likewise for G and B, with percentages brought between 0 and 1.
3. "name": the trade name as written in the document, 60 characters at most.
4. "pigment": the Colour Index code(s) (e.g. "PB29", "PR122/PV19"), 20 characters at most.
5. "light": lightfastness on the ASTM scale: "I" (excellent), "II" (very good) or "III" (not permanent). If the manufacturer uses another scale (stars, Blue Wool, letters…), don’t convert it: "".
6. "opac": "T" (transparent), "ST" (semi-transparent), "SO" (semi-opaque) or "O" (opaque), otherwise "".
7. "effect": "metal" if the manufacturer states a metallic paint (gold, silver, copper, bronze, metallic), "iri" if it is iridescent, pearlescent or interference, "fluo" if it is fluorescent, otherwise "" (ordinary paint or not stated).
8. File-level "group": the brand, 40 characters at most. If the document mixes several brands, add a "group" field in each tube instead.
9. One object per tube, in the document’s order, no duplicates (same name in the same group).

My document:

settings.excludeBlacksNote: On by default: a black tube is never suggested; black is mixed from colours (chromatic black).
settings.excludeBlacksWhy: Why? A tube black tends to look flat. A black mixed from colours (a dark blue and a brown, for example) keeps a warm or cool bias and blends better with the rest of the painting. And the tool only knows a tube’s colour: it can’t tell whether a black is already a mix. Blacks stay in your list, simply left out of the calculations.
settings.excludeEffects: No metallic, iridescent or fluorescent tubes
settings.excludeEffectsNote: On by default: metallic, iridescent, pearlescent or fluorescent paints are never suggested.
settings.excludeEffectsWhy: Why? A metallic or iridescent paint changes with the angle of the light, and a fluorescent paint emits light on top of what it reflects: a single colour on screen can’t represent them, and the computed mix wouldn’t be reliable. These paints stay in your list, simply left out of the calculations. The effect is detected from the name or pigment code; the tube’s “Effect” field corrects it.
settings.clearCacheNote: Removes the reference image, the chart and the selection. Your tubes are kept.
settings.cacheCleared: Images (reference and chart) and selection cleared. Your tubes are kept.
settings.backupTooBig: File too large (2 MB at most).
settings.backupNoValid: No valid tube in this file.
settings.replaceConfirm: Replace the {{current}} current tubes with the {{count}} from the file?
settings.wipe: Delete the data on this device
settings.wipeNote: Tubes, grid settings and image: permanent.
settings.wipeConfirm:
Delete all of this tool’s data on this device (tubes, grid settings, image)?

This can’t be undone. Consider exporting your tubes first.
settings.methodWarning: Results are indicative and can never be fully accurate. The only reliable judge is the objective perception of several people, in front of the real paint under the same light. The computer is only a calculating tool.

read: Exact RGB value of the pixel pointed at, in the image reduced to 1,600 px at most. It depends on the camera, the light, the screen and its profile: none of them is corrected here.
difference: Colours are converted to CIE L*a*b* (D65 white), then compared with the CIEDE2000 ΔE difference. Around 1, the difference is barely visible; beyond 5, it shows clearly.
mixing: Kubelka-Munk model, computed separately for red, green and blue. A tube is known only by its reference colour: its absorption (K/S) is derived from it, and its scattering (S) is estimated from its lightness. The calculation ignores real spectra, transparency and opacity, the binder, layer thickness and colour shift on drying.
search: Among the ticked tubes, the tool tries combinations of 1 to 3 tubes and looks for the proportions that minimise ΔE. The recipe shown has the best ΔE; if several match it (within 0.3, invisible), it keeps the one with the fewest paints. Proportions are relative parts. Other mixes are offered next.
blacks: By default, black tubes (named “black”, “noir”…, pigment only black PBk, or a very dark neutral colour) are left out of the calculations and the Advice: black is mixed from colours, as in the studio. Change it in Configuration, Calculation section.
effects: No metallic, iridescent or fluorescent tubes

By default, metallic, iridescent, pearlescent or fluorescent paints are left out of the calculations and the Advice: their look depends on the light (angle for metallics and iridescents, emitted light for fluorescents), which a single colour can’t represent. Change it in Configuration, Calculation section.
info: Information entered from the manufacturer’s sheet (lightfastness on the ASTM scale, transparency or opacity). Not used in the calculations: shown next to the tubes and the recipe. A mix’s lightfastness is that of its least lightfast tube.
cmyk: Simple conversion from RGB (1 − value), without a print profile.
chart: Average of a 5 × 5 pixel square, read on screen or on the zoom. For a PDF, the page is first drawn by the PDF reader, which converts CMYK colours to RGB approximately.
zone: On a PDF that contains text, the area drawn around is read straight from the PDF’s text (no character recognition): name, pigment code, lightfastness, transparency or opacity. Only the tube being added is filled in, and nothing is guessed. A reading can be wrong or pick the wrong line: always check before saving.
